working_title: North Norfolk's Golf Coast: A Practical Guide to Playing Hunstanton, Brancaster and Sheringham
angle: North Norfolk is England's most underrated links stretch for a UK golf trip — Royal West Norfolk (Brancaster), Hunstanton, and Sheringham sit within easy reach of each other along a short coastal corridor, yet they rarely appear in the same itinerary. The post treats the three as a coherent circuit, with honest practical notes on access quirks (tides at Brancaster, foursome-only format, weekend booking restrictions) that trip-planning articles typically gloss over.
research_notes:
- Royal West Norfolk Golf Club (Brancaster): founded 1892, laid out by Holcombe Ingleby, 6,457 yards, par 71. Little alteration to original design. Ranked 61st in the world among publicly-playable courses and 17th in England (Golf World). Located between Brancaster Bay and the salt marshes.
- Brancaster access quirk: the clubhouse is inaccessible at high tide — visitors must check tide times before travelling. The 8th and 9th holes are also affected by tides. The club itself advises checking tide times on their website.
- Brancaster format: two-ball course (singles and foursomes only); three- and four-ball play is not permitted. No weekend reservations or reservations during August for visitors — contact the Secretary directly for green fee rates.
- Hunstanton Golf Club: 18-hole, par 72, 6,741 yards, classic links designed by James Braid (1891). Out-and-back layout on either side of a central dune ridge. Described by top100golfcourses.com as 'a connoisseur's course jammed full of memorable quality golf holes.' Hosted the Brabazon Trophy and the British Amateur Championship. Visitors welcome; 36-hole day available with a supplementary fee listed on their website (£50 singles, £20 foursomes for second round — these figures are from the club website, confirm before publishing).
- Sheringham Golf Club: clifftop course on the North Norfolk coast, laid out by Tom Dunn in 1891, extended to 18 holes in 1898. Par 70. Bordered by the North Sea and the North Norfolk Railway. Has hosted English Women's Championships.
- Royal Cromer Golf Club: clifftop links, founded 1888, shaped by Old Tom Morris, J.H. Taylor, and James Braid. One of England's Royal clubs. Possible fourth course to mention for those with an extra day.
- Norfolk has the sunniest and driest climate in England — a genuine practical plus for UK golfers used to wetter west-coast conditions.
- Great Yarmouth & Caister Golf Club: oldest golf club in Norfolk, founded 1882, North Sea links that incorporates the Great Yarmouth racecourse as a hazard — worth a brief mention as a curiosity.
- Getting there: the north Norfolk coast is accessible from London/Midlands via the A10/A149 or train to Kings Lynn then car hire. No direct rail to Brancaster or Hunstanton — car is effectively required for the circuit.
- Tide tables for Brancaster are freely available from the UKHO/BBC Weather and the club website. This is a must-include practical note.
